What To Look For When SpaceX Reports Earnings (from UBS S&T)

SpaceX (SPCX) reports after the closing bell on Tuesday and heads into its first major earnings report as a public company with investor focus increasingly shifting beyond the quarter itself. While revenue and EBITDA performance will matter, the August 6 lockup expiration appears likely to be the bigger near-term driver, opening the door to the first meaningful wave of insider selling just days after results.

On the call, management is expected to spend considerable time on AI-related initiatives. Investors will be looking for updates on data center buildouts, potential increases to compute targets and any incremental commentary around Grok deployment timelines. Stronger-than-expected AI revenue could represent one of the more credible upside catalysts.

Beyond AI, attention will also center on Starlink and Starship. An updated Starlink subscriber figure could be disclosed, although the market may be hesitant to place significant weight on the metric while the network remains largely supported by V2 Mini satellites. For Starship, investors are likely to focus on execution milestones, launch cadence and any signals around the path toward operational payload launches.

Positioning remains an important factor. Hedge funds still screen as notably short, which could amplify upside if AI revenue exceeds expectations or if Starlink economics surprise positively, particularly around ARPU. Even so, the UBS desk believes the lockup expiration is likely to dominate the T+1 reaction and remain the primary stock-specific overhang in the near term.

Our new report "The Crowded Book" is live!

Why do crowded trades that fall together recover so differently?

Every rally needs continued demand. In a funded trade, that demand comes from cash flow or a supply sink that persists independently of price. Borrowed crowding relies on momentum and a thin float so demand weakens when prices stop rising.

The difference became clear in June. A sharp decline in Zcash triggered by a year-old exploit ignited a high-beta selloff across a weak market, pulling Hyperliquid and Venice down as well.

Hyperliquid’s recovery was supported by daily buybacks funded with 97% of trading fees and by a contributor team that kept restaking its unlocks instead of selling into them.

Zcash had no equivalent link to cash flow or usage. Its bid was based on scarcity, with the share of supply held in its shielded pool rising from roughly 8% to 30% over two years, backed by treasury vehicles accumulating alongside it. That steadily reduced the amount available to trade.

Venice had a growing product that most users could access without the token. Consumer growth did not translate directly into token demand. Relatively little supply was available to trade which made the price more sensitive to market flows in either direction.

That is why crowded trades that fall together recover apart. The recovery tests what was paying for the bid.

$HUT is down ~5.5% today after a squishy Q2 earnings landed alongside Gov. Abbott's Aug. 3 order freezing new Texas data center approvals pending a comprehensive ERCOT audit, which also paused the Batch Zero interconnection review.

The call told a more interesting story though: HUT's two flagship projects, River Bend and Beacon Point, are already contracted, financed with $7.5B in investment-grade non-recourse notes, and in active construction, so Abbott's audit doesn't really touch them. The pipeline (8.7 GW, 11 sites) is multi-state by design, and management flagged behind-the-meter power as potentially the fastest path to new capacity, which could sidestep the ERCOT queue altogether.

The Batch Zero pause could also be a net positive for HUT. They were one of the few companies to actually respond to the PUCT/ERCOT data center survey (only 28 of 377 did). Interestingly, management said they're seeing record M&A inbound from developers sitting on land and interconnect who need someone to commercialize it, exactly the kind of opportunity that shakes loose when weaker players get flushed out. CEO Genoot framed it as the platform beginning to compound. On supply chain tightness, management flagged no concerns , with the company pointing to CEO-level supplier relationships as insulation.

Stocks are a lot like relationships. When you find a great one, that’s where most of your capital should go. Yes, diversification has its place, but when you truly believe you’ve found your best opportunity, it should deserve your biggest allocation.

If I had to attribute my thousands of percentage points of outperformance over the market during the last 15 years to one thing, it would be this: when I find a great investment, I allocate most of my capital to it. In the past, I’ve done this with $ZIM twice, short $UVXY - multiple times, $VIX, more recently with $WGS, and $STAA.

Right now, $ZIM is approaching 40% of my portfolio. The stock is now trading around $27, up 17% from the $23 level where I recommended buying it aggressively. Some people will say, “It’s only up 17%.”

That’s true. But it’s 17% on what is now one of the largest positions in my portfolio. Position sizing matters.

It’s very rare to find a company trading at roughly half of its net asset value while currently printing money. As the Norwegian hedge fund that shorted $ZIM based on its calculations of how many new ships are being built and expectations for lower demand, and is now down 9% YTD, is learning, the future is up for grabs. The previous CEO avoided paying dividends and selling assets, instead hoarding cash and assets because he intended to buy the company himself, he is now out. We believe the new CEO will take a different approach, and he has plenty of room to work with.

With around $26 per share in cash, zero debt, and contracts that could potentially be sold for another $1–2 billion without jeopardizing the business, we expect a very different path for the company going forward.

Ironically, we also have to thank the previous CEO. By hoarding all that cash and those assets, which we believe was meant to help him acquire the company, he may instead end up handing them back to shareholders.

Life sure has a sense of humor.

Some countries move fast. Others slow themselves down with fear, regulation, or short-term thinking.

The Draper Innovation Index measures the rise and fall of innovation on a global scale. Where is the best place in the world for innovation and entrepreneurship?

Europe is being forced to pay up for oil getting tariffs from the US, and Denmark is being caught with a dilemma.

Canada is no longer quite so friendly to entrepreneurs and dropping on the index.

The middle east is having obvious conflicts which short term is bad for innovation, but possibly shows some long term hope.

Venezuela is showing promise to become more of a part of the innovation economy.

In 2025, we saw massive shifts driven by artificial intelligence, digital assets, and geopolitical change. AI alone is projected to automate 11.7% of global jobs, representing over $1.2 trillion in wages. But… AI is helping startups and entrepreneurship is growing rapidly.

Every major breakthrough feels threatening before it feels inevitable.

Electric cars looked impossible. Bitcoin wasn’t considered money. The internet wasn’t trusted. Now they’re part of daily life.

The DII isn’t about tracking trends, it's about looking forward to identify the environments where innovation has room to grow, and where entrepreneurs are free to experiment, fail, adapt, and lead.

Countries and states that protect economic freedom, encourage entrepreneurship, and invest in human capability consistently outperform those that don’t. The data makes that very clear.

If we want the next generation to thrive in a world shaped by AI, volatility, and rapid change, we need to understand where innovation flourishes, and why.

Explore the Draper Innovation Index in the comments

Entropy issues are not new in cryptocurrency land. 

In 2013, all wallets on Android suffered entropy issues as the operating systems RNG was not cryptographically secure. 

Around 2017 or so, RFC 6979 was adopted to replace the random number generator when producing a new digital signature with a deterministic scheme — as private keys can be leaked if poor randomness is used during the signing phase & publicly detectable onchain. 

The cold card entropy issue is tragic, but getting entropy right is still non-trivial. Mostly because it’s somewhat difficult to detect from the signature output without an active investigation.

Comparing Anthropic’s Fable to DeepSeek on price per token is a bit misleading. DeepSeek is genuinely very efficient, with MoE routing, fewer active parameters, low-precision weights, compressed attention and aggressive KV-cache optimization etc. Their chips are so bad (h200) that they became excellent at optimizing everything. 

BUT architecture is only part of the gap. DeepSeek also appears to be pricing strategically at extremely low margins, potentially close to marginal inference cost, to maximize adoption and utilization.

Anthropic is pricing the full economics of a frontier AI business: massive R&D, reserved capacity, enterprise reliability, compliance, support, safety infrastructure and a real (massive?) gross margin.

So this isn’t simply “the same intelligence is 100x cheaper.” It’s a comparison between different model classes, different infrastructure, and very different business strategies. DeepSeek is exceptionally cheap, but not uniquely so. Mistral Small 4 is nearly as cheap, and Gemini 2.5 Flash-Lite too which is probably a better comparison.

This is true. It’s still striking to me how many people expect AI compute prices to fall simply because new capacity keeps coming online.

The demand side is digital. The supply side is physical.

Demand can grow almost exponentially overnight especially as models improve. Supply is constrained by GPUs, HBM, power, transformers, electricians, data centers, permitting… (and a hundred other bottlenecks).

In this market, GPU prices are ultimately driven by the value they unlock, not just by the cost of the hardware.

So for example: 

Company A uses GPUs to summarize internal emails. Great, it saves thousands of hours so millions of dollars. 

Company B uses those same GPUs to discover a new drug or make a scientific breakthrough worth tens of billions. Company B will simply outbid Company A. 

As AI expands into more frontier use cases with enormous economic value, the willingness to pay for the newest compute keeps increasing. So even as supply grows, don’t be surprised if frontier compute remains expensive, or even gets more expensive!
